segments.t: German turns out to be a former boxing champion and easily floors all three chefs, but when a policeman walks into the alley, Barinov and German team up with a quick cover story.
Мы же коллеги, работаем в ресторане.
На спортзал у нас времени нет.
Вот мы на перерыве и боксируем.
Я вообще мастер спорта по боксу.
Let's go through each line of their improvised boxing excuse.
'Well, did we settle things like men?' Notice how Russian puts 'like a man' and 'to sort out, to figure out' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'I simply slipped.' Here Chef Barinov anchors the thought on 'simply, just' and finishes on 'to slipped', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'Right, a fight in a public place!' In everyday Russian, 'so, like this' flows straight into 'place' without extra linking words.
'Oh come on, what fight?' The exclamation 'what are you saying!' dismisses the officer's accusation with warm surprise.
Мы же коллеги, работаем в ресторане.
'We are colleagues, we work at the restaurant.' Barinov stresses their shared workplace using the first-person plural present tense.
На спортзал у нас времени нет.
'We have no time for the gym.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
Вот мы на перерыве и боксируем.
'So we box on our break.' Borrowed sports verbs in '-irovat' drop that suffix and take '-iruem' in the 'we' form.
'Yes, of course, we spar quite often.' German backs up the lie using the same '-uem' first-person plural verb pattern.
Я вообще мастер спорта по боксу.
'I am actually a Master of Sport in boxing.' Notice how Russian puts 'at all, even' and 'boxing' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'And my buddy helps me.' Here German anchors the thought on 'friend' and finishes on 'is helping', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'And what happened to the car?' In everyday Russian, 'the car' flows straight into 'happened' without extra linking words.
'Nothing serious, I have it insured.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
'You need to hold sparring matches in the ring.' In Russian, boxing happens 'on the ring' rather than 'in the ring'.

'All right then, all the best.' Here the inspector anchors the thought on 'only, in all' and finishes on 'good', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural. Now listen to the whole scene again from beginning to end.
Мы же коллеги, работаем в ресторане.
На спортзал у нас времени нет.
Вот мы на перерыве и боксируем.
Я вообще мастер спорта по боксу.

That wraps up this scene as after German easily knocks down Barinov, Senya, and Fedya, a police officer arrives and both chefs pretend they are simply colleagues boxing on their break. Until next time!
